2. In this writ petition, the petitioner made a prayer for directing the respondent No. 3 to hold investigation against respondent No. 1, 1A and 2 regarding the allegation made in the above report published in the above newspaper. The respondent No. 3 being the Director General of Bureau of Anti-Corruption is not supposed to hold any investigation himself. So, the prayer should have been to issue a direction upon the respondent No. 3 for taking steps for holding such investigation. In any case, the fact remains that the petitioner prayed for giving a direction for holding investigation about the allegation contained in the report published in the above newspaper. 

 156. (1) Any officer in charge of a police station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case which a Court having jurisdiction over the local area within the limits of such station would have power to inquire into or try under the provisions of Chapter XV relating to the place of inquiry or trial. 

 (2) No proceeding of a police-officer in any such case shall at any stage be called in question on the ground that the case was one which such officer was not empowered under this section to investigate. 

 157. (1) If, from information received or otherwise, an officer-in-charge of a police-station has reason to suspect the commission of an offence which he is empowered under section 156 to investigate, he shall forthwith send a report of the same to a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of such offence upon a police-report, and shall proceed in person, or shall depute one of his subordinate officers [not being below such rank as the [Government] may, by general or special order, prescribe in this behalf] to proceed, to the spot, to investigate the facts and circumstances of the case, [and, if necessary, to take measures 1 for the discovery and arrest of the offender: 

 (a) 	when any information as to the commission of any such offence is given against any person by name and the case is not of a serious nature the officer in charge of a police-station need not proceed in person or depute a subordinate officer to make an investigation on the spot: 

 (b) 	if it appears to the officer in charge of a police-station that there is no sufficient ground for entering on an investigation, he shall not investigate the case. 

 (2) In each of the cases mentioned in clauses (a) (b) of the proviso to sub-section (1), the officer in charge of the police-station shall state in his said report his reasons for not fully complying with the requirements of that sub-section, [and, in the case mentioned in clause (b), such officer shall also forthwith notify to the informant, if any, in such manner as may be prescribed by the [Government], the fact that he will not investigate the case or cause it to be investigated." 

 4. From the newspaper report, it appears that there are allegations of corruption and abuse of power mainly against respondent No. 1 and the offence, if any, comes within purview of the offence as contained in schedule to the [Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947] and schedule to the [Anti-Corruption Act, 1957]. Besides the above three sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure, there is also a provision for holding investigation regarding the offence contained in the schedule of the above two Acts. Under sub-section (2) of section 3 of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 an officer of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption has the power to make enquiry and to hold investigation of such offence as contained in the schedule to the Act. So. in the instant case, if it is found that order for holding investigation can be passed, the direction should be upon the respondent No. 3. 

 5. Now, the question is whether such an order can be passed directing the respondent No.3 to hold investigation about the allegations made in the report published in the above daily newspaper on 27-7-2001. In view of the provisions of sections 156, 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, normally there cannot be any investigation unless there is a first information report before the police officer concerned about commission of cognizable offence. However, under section 157(1) an officer-in-charge of a police station, if he has reason to suspect commission of an offence which he is empowered under section 156 to investigate, on receipt of any information or otherwise, the officer-in-charge shall proceed either in person or shall depute any officer to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances of the case. The use of the word "information' in section 157 normally means the information received under section 154 of the Code. In section 157, besides using the word ‘information, the expression or otherwise' has also been used. Now, this expression, according to us, cannot empower a police officer to start investigation on the basis of a report published in a newspaper. If a police officer is required to start investigation on a report published in a newspaper, this will create a hazardous situation in the whole society. Interested persons may publish a report in a newspaper with the sole purpose of harassment and even blackmail. 

 6. After perusing the provisions of sections 156, 157, we find that these contain enabling provisions giving power to the officer-in-charge of a police station to hold investigation in a case involving cognizable offence. Under section 156, an officer-in-charge may investigate a "cognizable case". The use of the expression "cognizable case" indicates that there must be a case which starts on the basis of an information. Publication of a report in a newspaper about commission of a cognizable offence against a particular person is not "information" within the meaning of section 154. The information on which the officer-in-charge of the police station may start investigation must be credible information received by such an officer either from a private person or from any intelligence source or agency. Even if there is a formal first information report, the police officer is not legally bound to hold investigation in view of proviso (b) to section 157(1). 

 7. To our knowledge the only precedence where this Court passed an order directing the officer-in-charge of a police station to hold investigation is the order passed in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 7226/2000. In that case, father of the victim wrote a letter to Mr Nirmal Sen, a political leader, alleging that police refused to record a first information report. Mr Sen then made an appeal to the Hon'ble Chief Justice by publishing an article in daily 'Janakantha'. Then the Hon'ble Chief Justice directed a Division Bench of this Court to pass necessary order. In that case, this Court directed the police authority to record the letter of the father of the victim as first information report and thereafter to hold investigation. As the police authority earlier refused to record first information report such direction was given. But in the instant case, no approach was made to the police authority and there was no refusal by such authority. 

 8. An order for holding investigation also may be given by a Magistrate under section 202 of the Code if a petition of complaint is filed before a Magistrate, and if he does not take cognizance under section 200 of the Code. But, for passing such an order, there must be a petition of complaint before the Magistrate. So, we find that either there must be some information before police officer about commission of a cognizable offence or there must be a formal complaint before a Magistrate for starting or holding investigation in a case of cognizable offence. 

 12. Mr Abdur Razzaque at last stage of his argument conceded that actually there is no allegation against respondent No. 2, the Registrar of this Court. The learned Advocate SN Goswami who appeared on behalf of the editor. printer and publisher of daily "Dinkal" has also conceded that there is nothing to show the involvement or collusion of the respondent No. 2, rather Mr Goswarni, after taking us through the relevant papers, has submitted that only a letter was issued by the Registrar of this Court for supplying computers for use of the Judges and officers of this court and the Registrar had no other involvement. He has referred to the letter at Annexure-"B". From this letter, we find that it was addressed to the Chief Engineer, Directorate of Works. We have also found that this letter was written by the Registrar under the direction of the authority. The Registrar is respondent No. 2 and appeared by filing affidavit-in-opposition. We find from annexure "x (i)" at page 20 that this letter was written with the approval of the Hon'ble Chief Justice. From the papers annexed with affidavit of compliance on behalf of the editor of the paper, we find at page 28 of annexure "B" that setting up of computers and fax machine were included in the revised PP as per desire of the Hon'ble Chief Justice. From the affidavit-in-opposition on behalf of the respondent No. 2, we find that the request for supplying computers was made to the Chief Engineer of the Public Works Department stating that such computers were necessary for use of the Judges and officers to clear backlog of cases and to expedite disposal of cases. So, in view of the papers submitted before us. both on behalf of the editor in compliance of the order of the court and by the respondent No. 2, it is clear to us that regarding purchase of computers the Registrar, respondent No. 2 had no involvement or participation. Naturally, for the above reasons, both the learned Advocates on behalf of the petitioner and on behalf of the editor frankly conceded that the respondent No. 2, had no involvement or collusion in the purchase and supply of computers to the Supreme Court. On perusal of the papers referred to above we have also found that actually respondent No. 2 had no involvement. So, the newspaper report to the effect that purchase of computers was done collusively by respondent Nos. 1 and 2 is absolutely without any basis.
